questions.q: What happens to the image if you make the pinhole very large?
questions.a: The image becomes blurry or disappears entirely because too much light enters from different angles, causing the rays to overlap. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks a larger hole acts like a "bigger window," not realizing that the sharpness of the image depends on the pinhole restricting light to a single, straight path.

questions.q: If you hold a pinhole camera to look at a tree, why is the image of the top of the tree at the bottom of the screen?
questions.a: Because light travels in a straight line from the top of the tree, through the pinhole, and continues in that same straight path to the bottom of the screen. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks the "camera flips it," missing the physical fact that the path of the light ray itself is responsible for the inversion.

questions.q: If an object is moved closer to the pinhole, what happens to the size of the image on the screen?
questions.a: The image becomes larger. As the object moves closer, the angle of the light rays passing through the pinhole increases, causing the projection to spread over a larger area on the screen. A wrong answer reveals the student hasn't visualized the geometry of the light paths converging at the hole.

questions.q: Why is the image formed by a pinhole camera called a "real" image?
questions.a: It is real because the light rays actually meet on the screen to form the image, rather than just appearing to originate from behind a mirror. A wrong answer shows confusion between "real images" (which can be caught on a screen) and "virtual images" (which cannot).

questions.q: Can a pinhole camera work if the box is not perfectly light-tight?
questions.a: No, because extra light entering from other gaps would wash out the faint image formed by the pinhole. Students who say "yes" do not understand that the image is a low-intensity projection that requires a dark environment to be visible.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment to prove that light travels in straight lines using a pinhole camera.
questions.a: Place two objects of different colors at different heights in front of the pinhole; if the images appear inverted and in the same relative order, it proves the rays crossed. A poor answer lacks a clear way to track individual light paths or fails to connect the inversion to the straight-line path.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A pinhole camera is a simple light-tight box with a tiny hole on one side that forms an ______, real image of an object on the opposite screen by allowing light to travel in straight lines.
Fill in the blank: Have you ever wondered how a tiny hole in a dark box can "______" a picture of the world outside?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to draw a ray diagram showing how light from the top and bottom of an object crosses at the pinhole to form an inverted image.
